query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thermally sprayed oxidation-resistant coating to the surface of a refractory or high-performance alloy will reduce oxide-scale growth at elevated temperatures compared to an uncoated control.
generation.material_initial_state: An uncoated high-temperature alloy (e.g., a refractory high-entropy alloy).
generation.intervention: Deposit an oxidation-resistant coating via thermal spraying to form a protective barrier.
generation.conditions: Exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air or combustion gases) at elevated temperatures (~1000–1200 °C) for extended durations (≥100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, adherent coating that forms stable oxide scales, slowing diffusion of oxygen into the underlying alloy.
generation.mechanism: The thermal-sprayed coating prevents direct contact between oxygen and the substrate, reducing oxide-scale growth and improving overall oxidation resistance by forming a slow-growing, protective scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significant decrease in oxide-scale thickness and mass gain, preserving mechanical integrity of the underlying substrate relative to an uncoated reference sample.
generation.baseline: Oxidation of an uncoated alloy under identical high-temperature conditions, leading to more rapid oxide-scale formation and greater mass gain.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness depends on coating composition, substrate preparation, coating quality, and thermal cycling conditions; suboptimal adhesion or mechanical spallation can compromise protection.
generation.uncertainty: There is limited data on the long-term stability of various coating formulations, especially under extreme temperatures and repeated thermal cycles.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of alloy samples, half coated with the thermal-sprayed oxidation-resistant composition and half uncoated. Subject both sets to identical oxidizing conditions (e.g., 1100 °C in air for 100 hours).
measurements: Measure mass changes (weight gain) repeatedly during exposure.
Perform cross-sectional SEM to measure oxide-scale thickness.
Evaluate microstructure and mechanical properties (hardness, tensile strength) of coated vs. uncoated samples post exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not display measurably lower oxide-scale formation or show similar oxidation damage and mechanical property degradation as the uncoated reference, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ].
